paper_metadata.title: Ductile L1 2Rh3Ti intermetallics for ultra-high temperature applications

All of the arc-melted alloys show clear fcc fundamental peaks as expected.

The arc-melted Rh –15Ti alloy contains evenly dispersed, equiaxed precipitates of 10 nm size as shown in the dark ﬁeld micrograph in Fig. 4a.
The arc melted Rh –20Ti alloy also consists of Rh3Ti precipitates in an Rh –Ti matrix as shown in the bright ﬁeld micrograph in Fig. 4b.
Transmission electron microscopy of the Rh –25Ti alloy revealed a single phase structure seen in Fig. 5 and superlattice re ﬂections in the diffraction pattern consistent with the L1 2 Rh3Ti phase.
The precipitates appear as discs about 50 nm in diameter and 20 nm thick. These discs are arranged orthogonally to each other in a three-dimensional network structure.
As shown in Fig. 7, the precipitate size increased to about 20 nm but no change in precipitate morphology is seen.

The selected area diffraction patterns of the Rh –15Ti alloy (shown in Fig. 4c) contained rings corresponding to fundamental as well as superlattice re ﬂections, which indicates that the precipitates solidi ﬁed incoherently within the matrix with no signi ﬁcant lattice matching.
These precipitates seem to solidify coherently with the matrix as indicated by the sharp spots in the selected area diffraction (SAD) pattern (Fig. 4d).
The bright ﬁeld and dark ﬁeld micrographs in Fig. 6b and c show the semicoherent precipitates containing what appear to be either fringes or interfacial mis ﬁt dislocations.
More importantly, the two phase Rh –15Ti alloy has signi ﬁcantly higher bend strength than the Ni-base superalloy.
Many L1 2 ordered phases exhibit an increase in ﬂow stress with increasing temperature making them attractive for high temperature applications [3].
